NOVELTY STATEMENT  
Standard practice delivers a MONITORING/INDICATION scheme using temperature thresholds to infer capacitor degradation. This proposal delivers a same-class MONITORING/INDICATION scheme using pressure differentials as a direct mechanical indicator of electrolyte loss, bypassing temperature inference and acting on the failure physics via boundary configuration. The pressure differential arises from gas generation during electrolyte decomposition, providing a direct measure of dry-out progression.  

PHYSICS CHECK  
Governing physical relation: Ideal gas law (PV=nRT) applied to sealed enclosure. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition increases internal pressure. Magnitude verification: For a 0.1L enclosure, 1% electrolyte decomposition (≈0.001 mol gas) at 60°C (333K) generates ΔP ≈ 27.4 kPa (CALCULATED: P=nRT/V = 0.001*8.314*333/0.0001). This exceeds typical pressure sensor resolution (1 kPa), making detection feasible.

- Maintenance: Same (no new maintenance routines).

EXECUTABLE TEST  
Protocol: Record pressure differential and temperature in 10 operational units for 6 months. Pass threshold: ΔP > 25 kPa at 60°C for >1 hour (validated against CALCULATED threshold). Kill criterion: If no ΔP spike occurs during known dry-out events (per historical data), mechanism falsified.  

CONSTRAINT BIND  
Primary stated indicator: Temperature (defines failure threshold in standard practice). This proposal uses pressure as a direct supplement to temperature, never replacing it. Pressure provides earlier detection of electrolyte loss before temperature rise manifests.  

RISK  
Pressure telemetry feed must be high-frequency enough to capture transient spikes; if data is low-resolution, signal may be missed.
